title: The Governor Who Became a Parliament and the End of Ordinance Raj
hook: After a state kept hundreds of temporary emergency ordinances alive for up to fourteen years without a legislative vote, the Supreme Court struck down the practice as a fraud on the Constitution.
laws: Constitution of India (Article 32, Article 123, Article 174, and Article 213)

facts.label: Court
facts.value: Supreme Court of India (Five-Judge Constitution Bench)

facts.label: Scale of Practice
facts.value: Two hundred and fifty-six ordinances promulgated in Bihar between 1967 and 1981 and kept alive for one to fourteen years by mechanical re-promulgation

facts.value: July 29, 1981 Parliamentary Affairs circular instructing departments to re-issue expiring ordinances without Cabinet approval if unchanged

summary: Between 1967 and 1981, the Governor of Bihar promulgated two hundred and fifty-six temporary ordinances and kept them alive for one to fourteen years by mechanically re-issuing them whenever the state legislature adjourned. One sugarcane ordinance was re-promulgated thirty-nine times over nearly fourteen years, and on multiple occasions more than fifty ordinances were re-issued in a single day without ever being placed before elected lawmakers for a vote.

An economics professor from Pune uncovered the pattern in official state gazettes and teamed up with a Ranchi farmer, a Patna college student, and a brick-business owner to file writ petitions under Article 32. During the hearing, the petitioners produced a July 29, 1981 government circular instructing departments to re-issue expiring ordinances before August 11, 1981 and explicitly stating that Council of Ministers approval was unnecessary if the text remained unchanged.

On December 20, 1986, a five-judge Constitution Bench rejected the State's objections on legal standing and mootness, holding that every citizen has a right to be governed by laws enacted in accordance with the Constitution. Declaring that a constitutional authority cannot do indirectly what it is forbidden to do directly, the court condemned mechanical re-promulgation as a colourable exercise of power and a fraud on the Constitution, struck down the Bihar Intermediate Education Council Ordinance, and awarded 10,000 rupees in costs to the researcher.

judgment.outcome: Writ petitions allowed; the Bihar Intermediate Education Council Ordinance, 1983 struck down as unconstitutional and void, with 10,000 rupees in costs awarded to the first petitioner.
points: Under Article 213 read with Article 174, a Governor's ordinance is strictly an emergency measure with a maximum lifespan of seven and a half months unless replaced by an Act of the legislature within six weeks of its reassembly.

Mechanically re-promulgating expired ordinances without submitting them to the elected legislature is a colourable exercise of power and a fraud on the Constitution, because a constitutional authority cannot do indirectly what it is forbidden to do directly.
Every citizen has sufficient public-interest standing under Article 32 to challenge a systematic executive practice that subverts constitutional lawmaking limits.

While courts do not inquire into a Governor's subjective satisfaction for a single emergency ordinance, they have full authority to strike down successive re-promulgations that usurp legislative power.

principles.name: Prohibition on Colourable Exercise of Power
principles.meaning: A constitutional authority cannot do indirectly what the Constitution forbids it from doing directly through a covert device or subterfuge.
principles.inThisCase: Re-issuing identical ordinances after each legislative session to bypass the six-week expiry limit under Article 213 was struck down as a fraud on the Constitution.

principles.name: Legislative Supremacy in Lawmaking
principles.meaning: Under India's constitutional design, primary lawmaking belongs exclusively to the elected legislature, while executive ordinances are narrow emergency exceptions.
principles.inThisCase: The bench ruled that the executive cannot convert an emergency power into a permanent parallel legislature or establish rule by ordinance.

principles.name: Citizen Standing to Enforce the Rule of Law
principles.meaning: Any member of the public has standing under Article 32 to challenge a systematic and flagrant violation of constitutional limits by the State.
principles.inThisCase: Even though the lead petitioner was an academic from Pune with no personal property affected, the court entertained his petition and awarded him costs.

takeaways: Temporary ordinances cannot exceed roughly seven and a half months without legislative approval.
Re-issuing an expired ordinance verbatim to avoid a legislative vote is unconstitutional.
Citizens can invoke public interest litigation to stop systematic executive overreach.

social.hook: How did one state keep temporary emergency ordinances alive for fourteen years without a single vote?
social.script: How did one state keep temporary emergency ordinances alive for fourteen years without a single vote? Between 1967 and 1981, Bihar's Governor issued 256 ordinances, re-promulgating them mechanically every time the legislature adjourned. One sugarcane ordinance was re-issued thirty-nine times, and an internal circular even told departments Cabinet approval was unnecessary if nothing changed. An economics professor from Pune uncovered the scheme in official gazettes and took it to the Supreme Court alongside affected citizens. On December 20, 1986, a five-judge bench condemned this Ordinance Raj as a fraud on the Constitution, struck down the surviving education ordinance, and awarded the professor 10,000 rupees in costs. You be the judge. Full case notes are on the Courtroom Chronicles website.
